title: Changes of State
full_text:
Hello and welcome back to JD Science.

In our previous lesson, we explored the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases.

Today, we are going to build on that knowledge by examining how substances change from one state to another.

We will explain melting, freezing, boiling, evaporation and condensation, and explore the role of energy in these processes.

Let us begin with a familiar example.

Imagine taking an ice cube from the freezer and placing it in a saucepan.

As the ice absorbs energy from its surroundings, its temperature increases until it reaches its melting point.

For pure water at normal atmospheric pressure, this is zero degrees Celsius.

At the melting point, the ice begins to change into liquid water.

But what exactly happens to its particles?

In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions. As energy is transferred to the solid, the particles gain energy and vibrate more vigorously.

At the melting point, the energy being supplied allows the particles to overcome enough of the forces holding them in fixed positions to move past one another.

The solid therefore becomes a liquid.

This process is called melting.

An important point to remember is that during melting, the temperature of a pure substance remains constant until the entire solid has melted, provided the pressure remains constant.

This is because the energy supplied is being used to overcome forces of attraction between particles rather than increasing their average kinetic energy.

Now, let us continue heating the liquid water.

As energy is transferred to the water, the particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.

Eventually, the water reaches its boiling point.

At normal atmospheric pressure, pure water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.

During boiling, bubbles of water vapour form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface.

The energy supplied enables the water molecules to overcome the attractive forces that keep them close together in the liquid.

The water changes into a gas.

Again, during boiling, the temperature remains constant until the liquid has completely changed into gas.

Now, you may be wondering: what is the difference between boiling and evaporation?

Both processes involve a liquid changing into a gas, but they occur differently.

Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid and can happen at temperatures below its boiling point.

For example, wet clothes can dry outside even when the temperature is only fifteen degrees Celsius.

This happens because some particles at the surface have enough energy to escape from the liquid into the air.

Boiling, on the other hand, occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

Now, let us reverse the process.

When water vapour loses energy, its particles move more slowly.

As they come closer together, attractive forces cause the gas to change into a liquid.

This process is called condensation.

You can observe condensation when water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass.

Water vapour in the surrounding air loses energy when it comes into contact with the cold surface and condenses into liquid water.

If liquid water continues to lose energy, it eventually reaches its freezing point.

At zero degrees Celsius, under normal atmospheric pressure, pure water begins to freeze.

During freezing, particles lose energy, and attractive forces hold them in fixed positions within the solid structure.

The particles continue vibrating, but they can no longer move freely past one another.

Let us now consider another change of state called sublimation.

Sublimation occurs when a solid changes directly into a gas without passing through the liquid state.

An example is dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide. At normal atmospheric pressure, it changes directly into carbon dioxide gas.

The reverse process, in which a gas changes directly into a solid, is called deposition.

Here is an important GCSE Chemistry principle.

Changes of state are physical changes, not chemical reactions.

When ice melts into water, no new substance is formed. The water molecules remain H two O.

Only their arrangement, movement and separation change.

These changes are also reversible.

Now, let us work through an examination-style example.

A student heats a sample of ice from minus ten degrees Celsius until it becomes steam at one hundred degrees Celsius.

Initially, the temperature of the ice rises as the particles gain kinetic energy.

At zero degrees Celsius, the temperature remains constant while the ice melts.

Once all the ice has melted, the temperature of the liquid water rises.

At one hundred degrees Celsius, the temperature remains constant again while the water boils.

This pattern produces a heating curve, which is an important graph in GCSE Chemistry.

Let us test your understanding.

Which change of state occurs when a gas becomes a liquid?

Condensation.

Which process occurs when a liquid changes into a solid?

Freezing.

And which process allows wet clothes to dry below the boiling point of water?

Evaporation.

Now, here is a GCSE examination question.

Explain why energy must be supplied when water boils. This question is worth three marks.

A model answer would be:

Water molecules are held close together by attractive forces. Energy must be supplied to overcome these forces so that the molecules can move farther apart and form a gas. During boiling, the temperature remains constant because the energy supplied is used to separate the molecules rather than increase their average kinetic energy.

Remember, the chemical bonds within the water molecules are not broken during boiling. It is the forces between the molecules that are overcome.

Thank you for watching, and I will see you in the next lesson.
